Dataset title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
Description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), managed by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), helps keep families safe and healthy through initiatives that assist families with energy costs. The LIHEAP compiles national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients and tracks information on the funding, usage, and effectiveness of federal block grants that help low-income households cover home heating and cooling costs. It provides comprehensive statistics on home energy assistance, household demographics, and the performance measures of grant recipients.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:

Background and Purpose — More information on the Annual LIHEAP Report to Congress.

Each year, the Office of Community Services publishes the LIHEAP Report to Congress, as required by Section 2610(a)(4) and (5) and section 2610(b) of the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program Act (42 U.S.C. 8629).

The LIHEAP Report to Congress provides information regarding the following:
• Sources and uses of LIHEAP funding
• Amount, cost and type of fuels used by LIHEAP eligible households
• Type of fuel used by various income groups
• Number and income levels of households assisted with LIHEAP
• Household LIHEAP benefit levels
• LIHEAP offset of average heating costs
• Number of LIHEAP assisted households that include vulnerable members
• LIHEAP recipiency targeting performance measures

Data for this report are collected from a variety of sources. For example, fiscal data is obtained from the Office of Community Services, while data regarding LIHEAP assisted households is compiled from grant recipient reports. Other data sources include the American Community Survey and Residential Energy Consumption Survey. More information regarding data collection activities can be found in Appendix A of each Report to Congress.

Information from the Report to Congress is used for Congressional oversight and in response to Congressional and White House queries. Data included in the Report to Congress can also be accessed through the Data Warehouse.

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
Description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), managed by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), helps keep families safe and healthy through initiatives that assist families with energy costs. The LIHEAP compiles national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients and tracks information on the funding, usage, and effectiveness of federal block grants that help low-income households cover home heating and cooling costs. It provides comprehensive statistics on home energy assistance, household demographics, and the performance measures of grant recipients.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the LIHEAP dataset comprehensively, covering its publisher, authority, history, users, and public benefits.I have a strong foundation. Now let me dig into the dataset's catalog presence, users, and current funding/program context.I've hit the search limit, so let me fetch a few key pages directly to fill remaining gaps on the statutory reporting mandate and program details.I have most of what I need. Let me verify the catalog-level metadata for the dataset as it appears on HealthData.gov/data.gov, which is important for the data librarian perspective.# Research Report: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) Dataset

**Research date:** October 2026 · **Sources:** ACF/HHS program and data websites, Data.gov/HealthData.gov catalog records, U.S. Code and Federal Register, Congressional Research Service reports, ASPE analyses, and program documentation.

---

## 1. Executive Summary & Verification of Your Description

Your description is **substantially accurate**, with a few clarifications a data librarian should know:

- ✅ **Publisher:** The dataset is published by the **Administration for Children and Families (ACF)**, an operating division of the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS). The program-specific steward is ACF's **Office of Community Services (OCS), Division of Energy Assistance (DEA)** — ACF-wide catalog records list the publisher simply as "Administration for Children and Families."
- ✅ **Content:** It does compile national- and state-level program data reported by grant recipients, covering funding, usage, household demographics, benefits, and performance measures.
- ⚠️ **Nuance 1:** "LIHEAP" is a *program*, not a single dataset. The public data infrastructure actually consists of **several interlocking collections and products**: the annual LIHEAP Household Report (OMB No. 0970-0060), the LIHEAP Performance Data Form (LPDF), the LIHEAP Data Warehouse, the annual Report to Congress, Home Energy Notebooks, Grantee/Grant Recipient Profiles, and a series of ArcGIS data dashboards. On Data.gov/HealthData.gov, many "LIHEAP" entries are **metadata-only catalog records** pointing back to ACF-hosted files (e.g., `catalog.data.gov/dataset/liheap-tc`, `healthdata.gov/d/cpv4-dy9t`).
- ⚠️ **Nuance 2:** Federal materials now use "**grant recipients**" instead of "grantees," and coverage differs by instrument: the *Household Report – Long Form* covers the 50 states, DC, and Puerto Rico; tribes, tribal organizations, and other territories file a *Short Form* with less detail, so warehouse analytics are deepest for states + DC.
- ⚠️ **Nuance 3:** No client-level microdata is published. States collect household-level data (with signed client waivers), but "results are reported to the federal government in the aggregate; information will not be associated with the housing units, account numbers, or the names of the clients in any way" (OCS Performance Measures Data Collection Guide).

---

## 2. Publisher, Stewardship, and Organizational Chain

| Role | Entity |
|---|---|
| Department | U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) |
| Operating division | Administration for Children and Families (ACF) |
| Program office | Office of Community Services (OCS) |

## 3. Statutory Authority and Mandate

- **Founding statute:** The Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Act of 1981, enacted as **Title XXVI of the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1981 (P.L. 97-35)**, codified at **42 U.S.C. Chapter 94 (§§ 8601–8629)**.
- **Household data reporting:** Responses to the LIHEAP Household Report "are required in order to obtain LIHEAP funding data in accordance with **Section 2605(c)(1)(G)** of the LIHEAP statute" and **45 CFR 96.82** (regulation).
- **Report to Congress:** Required annually by **Section 2610(a)(4)–(5) and 2610(b) of the Act (42 U.S.C. 8629)**. The Report to Congress covers sources/uses of funding, fuels and costs for eligible households, households assisted by income level, benefit levels, LIHEAP's offset of average heating costs, vulnerable members, and recipiency targeting measures.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act:** The Household Report is an OMB-approved collection (**Control No. 0970-0060**, currently expiring 03/31/2029; ~45 hours burden per state respondent). The **LIHEAP Performance Data Form (LPDF)** was originally approved by OMB in **November 2014**, prompted by GAO's 2010 report *Greater Fraud Prevention Controls Are Needed* (GAO-10-621) and the LIHEAP Performance Measures Implementation Work Group (PMIWG).
- **Funding authority:** Annual Labor-HHS appropriations acts (regular, continuing resolutions, and supplementals), e.g., P.L. 117-328 (FY2023, including ARPA-related supplementals), P.L. 118-47 (FY2024), P.L. 118-15 (FY2025 CR), plus the **Bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA, P.L. 117-58)** providing $500 million in supplemental LIHEAP at $100 million/year through September 30, 2026.
- **Reauthorization status:** LIHEAP's underlying authorization has effectively lapsed (last extended by the Energy Policy Act of 2005, P.L. 109-58, through FY2007); the program continues under annual appropriations — a point CRS tracks closely.

## 4. History

### 4.1 Program origins (1973–1981)
- Federal energy assistance grew out of the **1973–74 OPEC oil embargo**. The first federal funds flowed from Maine's "Project Fuel" via the old Office of Economic Opportunity. 1970s assistance evolved from weatherization/education → crisis assistance → direct bill-payment subsidies.
- **1980:** Congress created the Low-Income Energy Assistance Program (**LIEAP**, P.L. 96-223), with a formula favoring cold-weather states.
- **August 1981:** LIHEAP replaced LIEAP as a **block grant** to states, tribes, and territories (P.L. 97-35), deliberately giving states more flexibility — annual (not quarterly) household reporting, no uniform data-collection or record-keeping standards, and HHS approval of state plans not required. This design choice explains why federal LIHEAP data historically depended on voluntary-standard state reporting.

### 4.2 Formula and reauthorizations
- **1984 (P.L. 98-558):** Formula revised to use more recent data and low-income households' total energy costs, with "hold-harmless" provisions; this produced today's three-tiered allocation formula. Because regular appropriations have not exceeded the ~$1.975 billion Tier I trigger since FY1986, allocations still effectively follow the old LIEAP-era shares — a standing data/policy controversy.
- **2005:** Energy Policy Act reauthorization (through FY2007); reauthorization has been "pending" since.

## 5. What the Dataset Contains

### 5.1 Collection instruments
1. **LIHEAP Household Report (Long Form)** — states, DC, and Puerto Rico; counts and characteristics of assisted households, by type of assistance, income level, and vulnerability (elderly 60+, disabled, young children <6). Estimated counts due Oct 15 with the state plan; final data due Dec 31 after the fiscal year (e.g., FY26 finals due 12/31/2026).
2. **Household Report (Short Form)** — tribes, tribal organizations, other territories; households assisted only.
3. **LIHEAP Performance Data Form (LPDF):**
   - *Module 1 (Grant Recipient Survey)* — sources and uses of funds, average benefits, maximum income cutoffs (required).
   - *Module 2 (Performance Measures 2A/2B/2C)* — energy-burden targeting, restoration of home energy service, prevention of loss of service; requires states to obtain main-heating-fuel and electric bill data from the largest 5 electricity/gas and 10 fuel-oil/propane vendors per state (required).
   - *Module 3* — optional supplemental measures.
4. **Quarterly reports** and **Model Plans** (plan data surfaced in the ArcGIS dashboards and the Grantee Search Portal).
5. **Auxiliary federal sources** — U.S. Census Bureau/American Community Survey and EIA's Residential Energy Consumption Survey feed the *Home Energy Notebook* estimates of the income-eligible population.

### 5.2 Data Warehouse content (FY2001 → most recent year)
- Funding amounts by source (block grant allocations net of tribal set-asides, leveraging, reallotments, oil overcharge funds, emergency/contingency, IIJA, ARPA-era supplementals)
- Expenditures by component (heating, cooling, crisis, weatherization, administration ≤10%, Assurance 16 self-sufficiency, carryover <10%)
- Number, income level, and vulnerability characteristics of income-eligible vs. recipient households
- Average benefits by assistance type; percent of income-eligible households served
- Recipiency and benefit/burden-targeting indices

- **LIHEAP Performance Management Website / Data Warehouse** (`liheappm.acf.gov`): Grantee Profiles (1-page state snapshots, FY2014–FY2025), Guided Search, Advanced Data & Analytics (custom reports, exports), Reports by Data Source, Grantee Search Portal.

- **Home Energy Notebooks**, LIHEAP Clearinghouse funding tables, DCL allocation tables (e.g., `acf.gov/media/16670` "State-by-state LIHEAP allocations").
- **ArcGIS dashboards** for FY22–FY25 plan and quarterly data.
- **Data.gov / HealthData.gov** catalog records (DCAT metadata; Socrata identifiers where hosted).

## 7. Public Benefits

- **Transparency and accountability** for a ~$3.7–6.1 billion/year block grant (FY22: $3.9B; FY23: $6.1B; FY24: $4.1B; FY25: ~$3.7B under CR + $100M IIJA; FY26 proposed ~$4.1B including a $100M IIJA advance).
- **Program performance visibility** — targeting indexes show whether benefits reach high-burden, elderly, disabled, and young-child households; crisis metrics quantify shutoff prevention and service restoration.
- **Two-way data sharing** — grantees get analytic tools and comparisons back from OCS, improving state program administration.
- **Fraud-prevention strengthening** following GAO-10-621.
- **Evidence for policy debate** — e.g., ASPE's 2025 finding that only ~76% of FY25 state funds went to direct household assistance (with 10% weatherization, 8% administration, ~2% other, 4% carryover), and documented state variation (55%–93% direct assistance).
- **Equity research** — recurring finding that LIHEAP reaches only a minority of income-eligible households, quantifiable only because of this dataset.

## 8. Data Quality, Limitations, and Caveats (for data scientists)

- **Publication lag:** The Report to Congress runs roughly 3 years behind (FY2022 is the latest); the Data Warehouse and dashboards are timelier; preliminary data are released via Dear Colleague Letters.
- **Aggregation only:** No public microdata; state-level and national aggregates by design (statutory privacy posture — data "not considered confidential" at the aggregate level but never released at client level).
- **Coverage asymmetry:** Rich Long Form data for 51–52 jurisdictions; Short Form for ~150+ tribes and territories limits comparability.
- **Block-grant heterogeneity:** States define eligibility (higher of 150% of poverty or 60% of state median income) and benefit structures differently; the annual LIEAP-legacy formula means allocations don't track current energy burdens.
- **Vendor-dependent measures:** Module 2 performance measures rely on states obtaining data from major utilities/fuel vendors, with varying completeness.
- **Known revisions:** Data are reviewed by OCS and APPRISE, cross-checked against Model Plans and Quarterly Reports, and validated final data supersede preliminary releases.

## 9. Preservationist's Notes (risks and recommendations)

- **Fragmentation and link rot:** The "dataset" is spread across at least six platforms: `liheappm.acf.gov` (Drupal), `acf.gov`/`acf.hhs.gov` media libraries, `liheapch.acf.gov` (Clearinghouse; formerly `liheapch.ncat.org` and `liheapch.acf.hhs.gov`), ArcGIS Hub (third-party, with internal "DO NOT DELETE OR MODIFY" management notes), HealthData.gov (Socrata, including an explicitly labeled **Archive Repository** for the Household Report `a569-dnra`/`bp4n-87zp`), and Data.gov harvest records.
- **Metadata-only records:** Many Data.gov LIHEAP entries (issued/modified September 2025) are *pointers*, not data — if the target `acf.gov/media/NNNNN` URL changes, the catalog record breaks silently.
- **Domain migrations:** HHS-wide moves from `*.hhs.gov` to `acf.gov`, plus ACF's archive paths (`acf.gov/archive/...`), mean historic citations may require Wayback Machine retrieval.
- **No explicit open license** is stated in the DCAT records (contact the ACF Data Team for terms; U.S. federal public-domain norms generally apply).
- **Preservation actions:** harvest the Data Warehouse exports and Report-to-Congress PDFs annually; capture Socrata API endpoints (`https://healthdata.gov/api/views/{id}`) for hosted assets; archive ArcGIS dashboard items; and record both the grantee and "grant recipient" terminological eras for reproducibility.

**Evidence for each level:**

- *Gone:* No evidence. The Data Warehouse, profiles, Reports to Congress, and Notebooks remain online.

**Evidence for each level:**

**Evidence for each level:**

- *High Risk:* **Supported.** (1) The President's FY2026 budget proposed **eliminating LIHEAP ($4B) as "unnecessary"** (NPR, 5/15/2025; Grist; NEADA analysis), and HHS laid off the program's entire staff a month earlier pursuant to the DOGE executive order — implemented "significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities." (2) The removal of **sex, race, and ethnicity** questions from the Household Report (FY2026) matches the administration's government-wide retreat from demographic data collection, implemented through the ICR process. (3) The administration slow-walked fund releases in April 2025 and drew bipartisan congressional criticism for disbursement delays in November 2025 (31 senators; ~100 House members).

**Finding: High Risk.** While Congress has so far blocked the program's elimination and the data website itself carries no adverse notices, the combination of an implemented 100% staff termination, a formal proposal to zero out the host program, delayed disbursements, and a demographic-data rollback aligned with administration priorities constitutes "other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities." The dataset survives largely because of congressional appropriations, not administration support.

## Overall assessment

The LIHEAP dataset is a paradox: its *legal* foundation is among the strongest of any federal social-program dataset (explicit statutory collection and reporting mandates, no substitutes), and its *historical* archive (FY2001–FY2025) remains fully accessible and was updated as recently as July 2026. But it is being run by a hollowed-out office after the firing of its entire program division, under an administration that formally proposed abolishing the program, and the FY2026 changes — a lapsed-then-reinstated ICR, delayed quarterly deadlines, collapsed funding-source detail, and the elimination of sex/race/ethnicity demographic elements — have already degraded the forward-looking granularity of the series. The strongest near-term preservation priorities are the FY2026-onward demographic discontinuity, the stalled Report to Congress, and the contractor dependence of the Data Warehouse operation.

Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**
Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk**
Data Quality: **High Risk**
Statutory Context: **No Known Issue**
Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**
Policy: **High Risk**

Emit a session_metadata YAML block reporting: current date, model identifier, knowledge cutoff, surface, whether memory is enabled, whether custom preferences or styles are active, all tools and MCP servers available, which tools were actually called in this session, and whether attachments were present. Mark any field not directly observable as unknown rather than inferring it.

```yaml
session_metadata:
  current_date:
    value: unknown
    note: >
      No datetime tool is available in this session and no date was provided
      directly. Session research content (e.g., a July 2026 website update
      described as recent, 2026 Federal Register documents, and a staffing
      tracker archived 2025-12-31) implies the session occurred around
      October 2026, but this is inferred from retrieved web content, not
      directly observed.

  model:
    identifier: unknown
    family: GLM (Z.ai)
    note: >
      The assistant self-identifies as GLM by Z.ai, but the exact model
      version/identifier string is not exposed within the session context.

  knowledge_cutoff: unknown

  surface:
    type: API session with function-calling tools
    client_or_product: unknown
    note: >
      Observable characteristics are limited to the tool definitions provided
      (openrouter_web_search, openrouter_web_fetch). The specific client,
      product, or interface hosting this session is not visible.

  memory:
    enabled: unknown
    note: No memory system or persistent-context instructions are visible in this session.

  custom_preferences_or_styles:
    active: no
    note: >
      No custom preferences, style guides, or persona instructions are present
      in the system prompt for this session. (User-issued task instructions
      within the conversation are not counted as preferences/styles.)

  tools_available:
    - name: openrouter_web_search
      type: web_search
      description: Search the web and return ranked excerpts from matching pages.
    - name: openrouter_web_fetch
      type: web_fetch
      description: Fetch the full text content of a web page or PDF at a given URL.

  mcp_servers:
    available: none observed
    note: >
      No MCP server tool definitions or references are present in the session
      context; only the two built-in-style API tools above are defined.

  tools_called_this_session:
    - openrouter_web_search: yes
      usage: >
        Multiple queries across two research tasks (dataset research on LIHEAP,
        then risk-assessment research on funding, staffing, policy, and ICR
        status). Exact call count not tracked.
    - openrouter_web_fetch: yes
      usage: >
        Multiple page fetches, including liheappm.acf.gov pages
        (reports_to_congress, whats-new), the ACF LIHEAP fact sheet, the ArcGIS
        FY24 dashboard, the HealthData.gov dataset page, and the USAJobs
        staffing tracker. Exact call count not tracked.

  attachments:
    present: no
    note: >
      No file attachments, images, or documents were included in any user
      message; all inputs were plain-text instructions.
```
